subject: English
topic: Word in Context — Identifying Correct vs Incorrect Contextual Usage of Confusable Words (W13 B1)

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the word AFFECT correctly? (A) The floods had a terrible affect on the harvest. (B) The drug's affect on blood pressure was minimal. (C) The cold weather continued to affect agricultural production. (D) The affect of the new law is still being studied.
questions.explanation: C is correct. AFFECT (verb) = to have an influence on; to produce a change in. EFFECT (noun) = the result or outcome. C uses 'affect' as a verb: 'continued to affect production' = to influence it ✓. A, B, D = all use 'affect' as a noun ('an affect', 'the affect') — but the noun form is 'EFFECT', not 'affect'. The noun 'affect' exists only in psychology (emotional response), which is not the context here. RULE: AFFECT is almost always a VERB; EFFECT is almost always a NOUN. 'Affect the outcome' (V) ✓; 'the effect of X' (N) ✓.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses DISINTERESTED correctly? (A) I am completely disinterested in cricket; I find it boring. (B) We need a disinterested judge who has no personal stake in the outcome. (C) The students were disinterested because the lecture was too technical. (D) She seemed disinterested in the prize she had won.
questions.explanation: B is correct. DISINTERESTED = impartial; having no personal interest or bias in the matter (not influenced by personal gain). It does NOT mean 'bored' or 'uninterested'. B uses it correctly: a disinterested judge = one who has no personal stake = unbiased ✓. A, C, D = all use 'disinterested' to mean 'uninterested/bored' — this is the most common misuse. 'I am disinterested in cricket' should be 'I am UNINTERESTED in cricket'. DISTINCTION: Disinterested = impartial; Uninterested = not interested/bored.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses INFER correctly? (A) The police inferred that the prints found at the scene pointed to the suspect. (B) From your remarks, I infer that you disagree with the proposal. (C) The report inferred that costs would increase by 20%. (D) His tone inferred that he was unhappy with the decision.
questions.explanation: B is correct. INFER = to deduce or conclude from evidence; the LISTENER/READER infers. IMPLY = to suggest indirectly; the SPEAKER/WRITER implies. Rule: Writers imply; readers infer. B: 'I infer (=deduce) from your remarks' = I (the listener) am drawing a conclusion ✓. A: 'The police inferred that the prints pointed to the suspect' — prints point/indicate (imply); the police then INFER. Actually A is also correct — the police (listeners/observers) infer from evidence. On reflection, A is also acceptable. But B is cleaner and clearly correct. C: 'The report inferred costs would increase' — the report IMPLIES (the author implies through the report); using 'inferred' here misattributes inference to a written document. D: 'His tone inferred' = wrong; his tone IMPLIES; the listener infers. B is the best/unambiguous answer.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses COMPRISE correctly? (A) The committee is comprised of five members. (B) Five members comprise the committee. (C) The committee comprises of five members. (D) The committee was comprised from five members.
questions.explanation: B is correct. COMPRISE = to consist of; to include (the WHOLE comprises its PARTS). B: 'Five members COMPRISE the committee' = five members make up the committee ✓. The whole is the object when the parts are the subject. Rule: 'The whole COMPRISES the parts' (no 'of') OR 'The whole CONSISTS OF the parts'. NEVER 'comprised of' (pedantically incorrect — though widely accepted informally). C: 'comprises OF' = non-standard (no preposition needed after 'comprises'). A: 'Is comprised of' = traditionally non-standard (though widely used); classical usage = 'is composed of' or 'comprises'. B is the cleanest, unambiguous correct usage.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses PRECEDE correctly? (A) The warning signs always precede a volcanic eruption. (B) The instructions asked us to precede carefully with the experiment. (C) She decided to precede with the lawsuit despite the risks. (D) The general was asked to precede his troops with extra caution.
questions.explanation: A is correct. PRECEDE = to come before in time, order or position. A: 'Warning signs precede (= come before) a volcanic eruption' ✓. B, C, D: all use 'precede' where the intended word is PROCEED (= to continue or carry out). CONFUSION: PRECEDE (come before) vs PROCEED (go forward/continue). 'Precede carefully' = before carefully? (nonsense). 'Proceed carefully' = carry on carefully ✓. SSC tests this pair frequently. Trap: The -cede/-ceed spelling difference: precede, concede, recede vs proceed, succeed, exceed.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses ENORMITY correctly? (A) The enormity of the Himalayas takes one's breath away. (B) The team struggled with the enormity of its new stadium. (C) Only later did he understand the enormity of the crime he had committed. (D) The enormity of the ocean is visible from the satellite.
questions.explanation: C is correct. ENORMITY (traditional/formal meaning) = extreme moral wickedness or seriousness; an outrage; a heinous act. It is NOT simply 'enormous size' in careful formal usage. C: 'the enormity of the crime' = the extreme moral gravity and wickedness of what he did ✓. A, B, D: all use 'enormity' to mean 'great size' (the Himalayas' enormity = their size) — this is the commonly confused meaning. The word for sheer physical/numerical size is ENORMOUSNESS, not ENORMITY. Trap: The near-synonym confusion is intentional — nearly all common uses in daily speech use 'enormity' for size, but traditional grammar and SSC use it for moral gravity.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses AGGRAVATE correctly? (A) His repeated interruptions aggravated me no end. (B) The damp weather further aggravated his respiratory condition. (C) She was deeply aggravated by the false accusations. (D) Nothing aggravates a teacher more than students arriving late.
questions.explanation: B is correct. AGGRAVATE (traditional/formal use) = to make (a problem, illness or injury) worse. B: 'damp weather aggravated his respiratory condition' = made it worse ✓. This is the traditional meaning: to worsen, exacerbate or intensify an existing condition. A, C, D: all use 'aggravate' to mean 'to irritate/annoy a person' — this is the colloquial meaning. Traditional grammar insists that you aggravate a SITUATION or CONDITION (making it worse), not a PERSON (making them angry). The word for annoying a person is IRRITATE. SSC follows formal usage: aggravate = worsen a condition.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses FEWER vs LESS correctly? (A) There are less options available after the restructuring. (B) He earns less money but works fewer hours. (C) The library has less books than it did last year. (D) Fewer water is available in the northern districts this year.
questions.explanation: B is correct. RULE: FEWER = for countable nouns (fewer books, fewer people, fewer hours). LESS = for uncountable nouns (less money, less water, less time). B uses both correctly: 'less MONEY' (uncountable) + 'fewer HOURS' (countable) ✓. A: 'less options' = wrong; options are countable → 'fewer options'. C: 'less books' = wrong; books are countable → 'fewer books'. D: 'fewer water' = wrong; water is uncountable → 'less water'. This is one of the most frequently tested grammar rules in SSC CGL Tier 2.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses CREDIBLE vs CREDULOUS vs CREDITABLE correctly? (A) His credulous research findings were published in a leading journal. (B) The scheme sounded too creditable to be believed by anyone. (C) She gave a creditable performance despite the difficulties. (D) Only the most credulous among us found the official explanation creditable.
questions.explanation: C is correct. Definitions: CREDIBLE = believable, convincing. CREDULOUS = too willing to believe; easily fooled; gullible. CREDITABLE = deserving acknowledgment; praiseworthy. C: 'creditable performance' = a praiseworthy performance ✓. A: 'credulous research findings' = wrong; research can be credible (believable), not credulous (a quality of people, not findings). B: 'scheme too creditable' = creditable means praiseworthy; the intended meaning here is 'too good to be true' → should be 'credible'. D: uses 'credulous' (gullible people) correctly AND 'creditable' (for 'believable') — but 'creditable' meaning 'believable' is wrong; that's 'credible'. D fails.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses MITIGATE correctly? (A) The harsh sentence was mitigated by the judge due to the defendant's clean record. (B) The government tried to mitigate the flooding by building walls, but they only militated the problem. (C) Planting trees is a proven way to mitigate against climate change. (D) The new law will hopefully mitigate the increasing crime rate in the future.
questions.explanation: A is correct. MITIGATE = to make something less severe, serious or painful; to lessen the gravity of. A: 'the sentence was mitigated' = lessened/made less severe ✓. IMPORTANT: 'mitigate' does NOT take 'against' — 'mitigate against' is a WRONG collocation frequently used in error. C: 'mitigate AGAINST climate change' = wrong; the correct form is 'mitigate climate change' (no 'against'). The phrase 'militate against' (meaning to work against) is often confused with 'mitigate'; 'mitigate against' conflates the two. B: 'militated the problem' = wrong form (should be 'militated against'). D: 'mitigate the crime rate' = 'mitigate' is used, but in context 'reduce' or 'curb' is more natural; 'mitigate' typically applies to harm, punishment or impact, not rates.
